report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Background: Buprenorphine offers an analgesic option for selected adults with chronic pain.
National trends in pain-indicated buprenorphine prescribing, variation across state policy approaches, and consistency within multiple insurance payers have not been examined together.
We described national and state prescribing trends, compared growth among states with documented policies, and examined whether state patterns persisted among Medicaid recipients.

Methods: Longitudinal ecological analysis of 2017-2025 prescription claims for 867,591 unique adults receiving transdermal or buccal buprenorphine across 888 three-digit ZIP code areas, with a systematic policy review of the 50 states and District of Columbia.

Outcomes were annual recipients of painindicated formulations per 100,000 adults, observed and modeled with a hierarchical Bayesian model (95% credible intervals), state policy characteristics, and payer-restricted rates.
The observed national rate increased from 53.59 to 78.04 recipients per 100,000 adults (45.6%; 4.81% annualized); model-derived average annual growth was 5.04% (95% credible interval, 2.88%-7.28%).
The policy review identified distinct guidance, coverage, oversight, and educational approaches.
Annualized growth was 25.43% in Minnesota, 13.50% in Colorado, 6.29% in North Carolina, 3.35% in Virginia, 2.99% in California, 0.63% in West Virginia, 0.50% in Oregon, and -2.96% in Mississippi.

Identifiable-Medicaid prescribing grew 3.10% annualized nationally versus 4.81% for all payers and increased in Colorado and Minnesota, but declined in Virginia and North Carolina, where plan coding and managed-care transitions limited Medicaid identification.
Conclusions: Prescribing increased nationally but varied substantially across states with different policy approaches, and Medicaid-restricted patterns did not consistently mirror all-payer trends.
Policy content, timing, and payer reach warrant evaluation; however, these ecological comparisons do not establish causation.
Chronic pain is common in the United States, and clinicians must balance symptom relief, function, and medication-related harm [1].
text.formatted: Chronic pain is common in the United States, and clinicians must balance symptom relief, function, and medication-related harm <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: For selected adults, buprenorphine offers analgesia with lower respiratory-depression risk than full-agonist opioids, although it remains an opioid with important risks [2] [3] [4].
text.formatted: For selected adults, buprenorphine offers analgesia with lower respiratory-depression risk than full-agonist opioids, although it remains an opioid with important risks <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Understanding who receives pain-indicated formulations, and how prescribing varies geographically, can identify questions about access that aggregate opioid statistics do not resolve.
The national context for opioid prescribing changed during the past decade.
The 2016 CDC guideline favored nonopioid therapy for chronic pain, and the 2022 update discussed transition to buprenorphine for selected patients [5, 6].
text.formatted: The 2016 CDC guideline favored nonopioid therapy for chronic pain, and the 2022 update discussed transition to buprenorphine for selected patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: How national guidance reaches practice depends partly on state medical boards, health departments, and insurers, which may influence prescribing through clinical guidance, coverage, prescribing rules, and education [7, 8].
text.formatted: How national guidance reaches practice depends partly on state medical boards, health departments, and insurers, which may influence prescribing through clinical guidance, coverage, prescribing rules, and education <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: Much buprenorphine policy research has focused on opioid use disorder (OUD), whereas painindicated formulations carry different costs and access requirements [9] [10] [11] [12].
text.formatted: Much buprenorphine policy research has focused on opioid use disorder (OUD), whereas painindicated formulations carry different costs and access requirements <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: A recent Medicaid study examined 2015-2024 prescription trends using coverage restrictions classified in August 2025 [13].
text.formatted: A recent Medicaid study examined 2015-2024 prescription trends using coverage restrictions classified in August 2025 <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Less is known about how all-payer prescribing has changed nationally, how growth varies among states with different policy content and timing, and whether state patterns hold within Medicaid, the payer that many state policies directly reach.
We therefore addressed three linked questions using national prescription claims and a policy review of all 50 states and the District of Columbia.

First, we described national trends and geographic variation in pain-indicated buprenorphine prescribing from 2017 through 2025, hypothesizing that prescribing would increase but that growth would vary across US regions and states.
Second, we characterized state approaches to clinical guidance, coverage, prescribing oversight, and education, and compared observed growth among states with documented policies.
Third, because many of these policies govern Medicaid coverage or oversight, we examined whether all-payer state patterns persisted among identifiable Medicaid recipients.
We conducted a longitudinal ecological analysis of 2017-2025 prescription claims and a policy review covering all 50 states and the District of Columbia.
The analysis proceeded in three stages: national and geographic prescribing trends, state policy review with state-level comparisons, and payer-restricted analyses.
Policy review used the READ framework [14].
text.formatted: Policy review used the READ framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Reporting was guided by STROBE (Table A in S1 Appendix) [15].
text.formatted: Reporting was guided by STROBE (Table <ref type="table">A</ref> in S1 Appendix) <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: The Wake Forest University School of Medicine Institutional Review Board (IRB00127502) determined that the study, which used deidentified prescription claims, was exempt from review and waived the requirement for informed consent.
We used the IQVIA Longitudinal Prescription Claims (LRx) database, which contains deidentified prescription records with patient age and three-digit ZIP code (ZIP3).
Data was first accessed on September 21 st , 2023 and last accessed on September 6 th , 2026.
IQVIA reports that LRx captures approximately 94% of retail, 82% of mail-service, and 74% of long-term-care prescription claims; coverage varies by channel and over time [16, 17].
text.formatted: IQVIA reports that LRx captures approximately 94% of retail, 82% of mail-service, and 74% of long-term-care prescription claims; coverage varies by channel and over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17]</ref>.

text.text: We identified transdermal patches and buccal films by National Drug Code and verified their FDA-approved indications (Table C in S1 Appendix).
text.formatted: We identified transdermal patches and buccal films by National Drug Code and verified their FDA-approved indications (Table <ref type="table">C</ref> in S1 Appendix).

text.text: Throughout the study, "pain-indicated" describes a formulation approved for pain, not a diagnosis confirmed in the claims; off-label use of OUD formulations for pain was outside the study definition.
We included adults aged 18 years or older and removed duplicate recipients within each year.
The outcome was the annual number of unique recipients per 100,000 adults.
The hierarchical model used fixed 2022 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year adult population estimates aggregated to ZIP3 areas; a sensitivity model used fixed 2017 estimates [18].
text.formatted: The hierarchical model used fixed 2022 American Community Survey (ACS) five-year adult population estimates aggregated to ZIP3 areas; a sensitivity model used fixed 2017 estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18]</ref>.

text.text: The separate observed-rate analyses used year-matched ACS five-year releases for 2017-2024 and the 2024 denominator for 2025.
Each ACS five-year release summarizes a rolling five-year period, not a single-year population survey.
The authors had no access to information that could identify individual participants during or after data collection.

We analyzed annual recipient counts using a hierarchical Bayesian Poisson model that allowed starting rates and growth to differ among ZIP3 areas while sharing information within states and nationally [19].
text.formatted: We analyzed annual recipient counts using a hierarchical Bayesian Poisson model that allowed starting rates and growth to differ among ZIP3 areas while sharing information within states and nationally <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[19]</ref>.

text.text: The state-level hierarchy included Medicaid expansion status for intercepts and slopes.
The model assumed constant proportional change within each ZIP3 area.
We converted fitted log-slopes to annual percentage growth with 95% credible intervals (CrIs).
The modelbased national summary used the unweighted arithmetic mean of fitted intercept and slope coefficients across the analytic geographic areas.
It includes jurisdictions with and without explicit recognition and is distinct from the observed population-weighted national rate.
Model specifications and diagnostics appear in the S1 Appendix.
Observed national and state rates used annual unique recipients and year-matched adult populations.

Because ZIP3 areas can cross state boundaries, Census ZCTA-county relationships and residential shares from the June 2026 HUD-USPS crosswalk informed ZIP3-to-state allocation, with year-specific ACS adult-population weights [18, 20].
text.formatted: Because ZIP3 areas can cross state boundaries, Census ZCTA-county relationships and residential shares from the June 2026 HUD-USPS crosswalk informed ZIP3-to-state allocation, with year-specific ACS adult-population weights <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">20]</ref>.

text.text: A recipient with multiple valid ZIP3 records contributed one total person after normalizing state weights.
The national comparator divided unique mapped recipients by the combined allocated adult population of the 50 states and DC.
Sensitivity analyses held 2024 populations constant or assigned each recipient to the state with the largest cumulative geographic weight.
Tables J-M in S1 Appendix report rates, rankings, sensitivity results, and completeness.
Two investigators (M.C.B.A. and R.W.H.) reviewed medical board policies, state-issued or stateendorsed guidelines, Medicaid pharmacy documents, and legislation across all 51 jurisdictions.
They independently adjudicated policy evidence using an evidence-level decision log; a third investigator (C.M.) was designated to resolve disagreements.
Explicit clinical recognition required a recommendation or preference for buprenorphine as an analgesic.
Institutional guidance without state endorsement, unenacted proposals, and workers' compensation-only policies were outside the policy scope (Table B in S1 Appendix).
text.formatted: Institutional guidance without state endorsement, unenacted proposals, and workers' compensation-only policies were outside the policy scope (Table <ref type="table">B</ref> in S1 Appendix).

text.text: We characterized clinical guidance, coverage, prescribing oversight, and education.
The review focused on 2014-2023, retaining earlier provisions and updates through 2025.
We distinguished document publication, legal effective dates, and clinical uptake.
Routine formulary placement was recorded as coverage, even when it did not meet the rubric for enhanced access.
Policies with different payer reach or clinical purposes were not combined into a single treatment exposure (Tables B, D, E, and I in S1 Appendix).
From the nationwide review we selected eight states to illustrate the range of documented approaches and their timing relative to follow-up.

Colorado illustrated clinical guidance, coverage, and education; Minnesota and California illustrated clinical guidance, prescribing oversight, and education; and Oregon illustrated clinical guidance and education.
Virginia illustrated clinical guidance and coverage policies.
Mississippi and West Virginia illustrated Medicaid formulary approaches that originated before follow-up, and North Carolina illustrated routine coverage without an enhanced pain-specific pathway.
These states are examples drawn from the full review, not a representative sample of jurisdictions.
We ranked all 51 jurisdictions by annualized observed growth and compared the illustrative states with the national comparator.

We also fitted additional Bayesian log-rate trends to the 2017-2025 observed series for each jurisdiction and the nation, using year-varying denominators and autoregressive residuals; these models supplement the hierarchical ZIP3 model (Table N in S1 Appendix).
text.formatted: We also fitted additional Bayesian log-rate trends to the 2017-2025 observed series for each jurisdiction and the nation, using year-varying denominators and autoregressive residuals; these models supplement the hierarchical ZIP3 model (Table <ref type="table">N</ref> in S1 Appendix).

text.text: For dated policy actions, we compared the last full pre-event year with the first full post-event year and the corresponding change in the pooled remaining jurisdictions.
We omitted partial implementation years and used a second comparator excluding 15 policy examples or candidates (Table H in S1 Appendix).
text.formatted: We omitted partial implementation years and used a second comparator excluding 15 policy examples or candidates (Table <ref type="table">H</ref> in S1 Appendix).

text.text: In additional analyses, we modeled the log ratio of Colorado to rest-of-US rates with seasonal terms and autoregressive errors and examined nominated breaks in January 2018 and January 2023.
Sensitivities used alternative break dates around documented changes and alternative model assumptions (Table G in S1 Appendix).
text.formatted: Sensitivities used alternative break dates around documented changes and alternative model assumptions (Table <ref type="table">G</ref> in S1 Appendix).

text.text: Annual segmented comparisons addressed Colorado, California, and Oregon when at least three full pre-and post-event years were available (Table Q in S1 Appendix).
text.formatted: Annual segmented comparisons addressed Colorado, California, and Oregon when at least three full pre-and post-event years were available (Table <ref type="table">Q</ref> in S1 Appendix).

text.text: Consistent with other opioid-policy evaluations, we distinguished implementation dates and examined comparison trajectories [48, 49]; we did not pool heterogeneous guidance, coverage, and educational actions into a single staggered intervention.
text.formatted: Consistent with other opioid-policy evaluations, we distinguished implementation dates and examined comparison trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[48,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">49]</ref>; we did not pool heterogeneous guidance, coverage, and educational actions into a single staggered intervention.

text.text: Because many state policies apply specifically to Medicaid, all-payer rates could dilute associations concentrated among Medicaid recipients or, conversely, could rise while prescribing for the targeted payer changed little.
We therefore examined whether all-payer patterns persisted among Medicaid recipients.
Payer-restricted analyses covered 2017-2025, using patient and plan dictionaries for the corresponding records.
Identifiable Medicaid comprised fee-for-service and explicitly identified managed Medicaid plans; a narrower analysis used fee-for-service only.
Mixed Medicaid/Medicare categories were not automatically classified as Medicaid.
Rates used adult population, not Medicaid enrollment, as the denominator, so payer-restricted rates describe recipients per adult resident rather than per enrollee (Tables O and P in S1 Appendix).
Generative artificial intelligence tools were used during manuscript preparation as follows.
Claude assisted with editorial revision of text (spelling and grammar), initial web searching for state policy sources, and initial figure and table preparation.

Policy sources identified with AI assistance were retrieved and independently supplemented and adjudicated against the original documents by M.C.B.A. and R.W.H. AI tools did not generate or alter any data, model estimates, or values shown in figures or tables.

All AI-edited output was reviewed and confirmed by the authors, who take responsibility for all hypotheses, interpretations, results, conclusions, and limitations, for the accuracy of all statements, and for the citation of all sources.

Pain-indicated buprenorphine prescribing increased nationally from 2017 to 2025, supporting our hypothesis, but growth differed substantially across regions and states.

A nationwide policy review identified several approaches that could influence access, yet states with documented policies had markedly different trajectories, and Medicaid-restricted patterns diverged from allpayer patterns in some of those states.

The central finding is therefore a national increase accompanied by geographic heterogeneity that was not consistently related to the presence of a documented policy and that depended in part on which payers were examined.

This national increase in buprenorphine for pain occurred while overall opioid analgesic prescribing declined and buprenorphine initiation for OUD was relatively flat during much of the overlapping period [50, 51].

Comparisons must also account for the starting prescribing rate, covered formulations, and payer reach: a policy introduced before 2017 may already have influenced the baseline, whereas a later Medicaid provision reaches only part of the population directly.

text.text: For clinicians and policymakers, the geographic differences identify questions about whether guidance is clear, coverage is workable, and education addresses analgesia as well as OUD.
Regional prescribing culture, pain burden, clinician supply, and insurance arrangements may also contribute.
These findings support evaluating access alongside treatment appropriateness, pain relief, function, and safety; greater dispensing alone does not establish better care.

Pain-indicated buprenorphine prescribing increased nationally with substantial state and regional variation.

A nationwide policy review identified diverse approaches to clinical guidance, coverage, oversight, and education alongside widely differing prescribing trajectories, and Medicaid-restricted patterns did not consistently mirror all-payer trends.
These findings support time-specific evaluation of how policy design, implementation, and payer reach influence access to buprenorphine for pain.
